absorptionBoosters: dietary fat or oil in the same meal
cooking greens (sauteing, steaming, pressure cooking) to break cell walls
eating greens with dal, curd or paneer
normal bile flow and fat digestion
absorptionBlockers: fat-malabsorption conditions (coeliac disease, IBD, liver or pancreatic disease, after bariatric surgery)
light exposure during storage of oils
warnings: Blood thinners (warfarin-type vitamin K antagonists): keep vitamin K intake steady from day to day and do not start, stop or change any vitamin K supplement, including D3 + K2 or calcium + K2 combinations, without your doctor.
No formal upper limit is set for vitamin K; UK guidance considers up to 1000 µg per day from supplements unlikely to cause harm in adults.
Vitamin K3 (menadione) is not used in human supplements because it can harm the liver.
Unexplained bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, very heavy periods or blood in urine or stool should be checked by a doctor.
Newborns need the vitamin K injection at birth as per Government of India guidelines; any bleeding in a baby needs urgent medical care.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: take vitamin K supplements only if a doctor advises them.
General information, not medical advice. Check with a doctor before starting supplements.
